title: Recording Loss and Rebuilding Community Memory in Łódź
summary: The historical commission, Jewish Committee, and memorial proposal show how survivors worked to document loss and preserve Łódź Jewish memory.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Memorial for the murdered Lodz Jews

editorialContent:
## A city returned to, and searched for

When the war ended, survivors came back to Łódź from camps, forests, hiding places and other liberated areas. Some hoped to find relatives; some sought to reclaim property; others tried to begin again. But return did not mean restoration. The destruction of the ghetto had left only a remnant of the city’s Jewish population, and each inquiry about a former resident carried the possibility of an answer—or of learning that there would be none.

The US Holocaust Memorial Museum places this return against the scale of the catastrophe: it describes Łódź as Poland’s second-largest prewar Jewish community and records that only a small number of Jews remained in the city when Soviet forces liberated it on January 19, 1945. Its account of survivor Blanka Rothschild, who returned hoping to find family and found none alive, gives one individual shape to the wider ordeal. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/lodz))

The Yiddish memorial book recalls postwar Łódź through practical acts of rebuilding as well as remembrance. The [Jewish Committee of Łódź](/communities/lodz/records/mention_3ed0055ccf6b8e7821e3cea1) received inquiries about former residents. The [Jewish Committee](/communities/lodz/records/mention_43edff7ab64e502948088fcc) also provided aid and worked on family-reconnection efforts. Those tasks belonged to a broader effort to make life possible again: the community organized schooling, relief and a [Repatriant House](/communities/lodz/records/mention_a78343a792953211dd54b9f4), while the Joint supplied material assistance. The book also recalls cultural revival, including the return of [Yiddish theater in Łódź](/communities/lodz/records/mention_355d77f01d046342500ea97d), with performers such as [Ida Kaminska](/communities/lodz/records/mention_766b848567e95dc9d372eaa7).

## Testimony as an answer to erasure

The memorial book describes the [Jewish Historical Commission](/communities/lodz/records/mention_b4a06fa450f3de22b4f31fab) as an institution that gathered survivors’ testimony. It names Dr. Philip Frirman as its leader, and identifies Dr. Kermish and M. Blumental among those recording survivors’ accounts. These are not merely names in an institutional history: they indicate the labor of listening, collecting and preserving recollections while survivors were still trying to locate family members and reassemble their lives.

The book places the commission at Narutowicza Street 29. A different JewishGen translation of a Lodz memorial text says the Central Jewish Historical Commission’s first seat was at Narutowicz Street 25. These accounts may refer to different offices or reflect a discrepancy in recollection or translation; the evidence available here does not settle it. The difference should remain visible rather than be smoothed into a single address. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lodz1/lode007.html))

The wider historical record confirms that postwar documentation was not unique to Łódź. Yad Vashem notes that a Jewish Historical Commission operating in Poland immediately after the war gathered testimony about the Jedwabne affair; those materials are held in the Jewish Historical Institute in Warsaw. That example supports the broader context of survivor documentation, but it does not independently verify the Łódź book’s account of Frirman, Kermish or Blumental. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/microsoft%20word%20-%204795.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## Inquiries, relief and a changing city

Questions about former residents were part of a painful everyday reckoning. An inquiry might reconnect a survivor with a relative, or bring news of a death far from Łódź. A community office could help people search, but no single committee could know the fate of everyone who had lived in the city. Survivors were scattered across countries and camps; many did not return, and many family lines had been destroyed. The memorial book captures the local work of answering questions, while the wider record warns against treating its lists or remembered accounts as complete.

Rebuilding also meant providing food, schooling, shelter and work. The book remembers the Committee’s connection to the first Jewish school in Łódź, and the Joint’s role in relief. A JewishGen translation of another Lodz memorial account describes how the Committee helped returning Jews seek housing and employment, and how institutions developed in the city as survivors arrived. It also notes that Łódź briefly became a center for Jewish organizations because Warsaw had been devastated. These details illuminate the setting for memory work: documentation took place amid urgent efforts to establish a livable present. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lodz1/lode007.html))

The institution’s own history continued beyond its first postwar work. The memorial book says that the Jewish Historical Institute later assumed the commission’s function and names Ber Mark as its leader. That succession links the urgent collection of testimony in postwar Poland with the longer preservation and study of Jewish historical records. It does not mean, however, that every story or inquiry was captured. The archive grew through choices about what survivors could tell, what workers could record, and what materials survived.

## A memorial proposed, and memory carried forward

The book also records a proposal to erect a modest memorial to the murdered Jews of Łódź. The surviving OCR renders the phrase for the memorial as a line-broken, uncertain fragment, so the wording and precise form of the proposal cannot safely be reconstructed from that excerpt alone. What can be said is that the idea appears in the book as part of a postwar effort to give public form to loss. The memorial was not only a monument; it was a claim that the murdered belonged to the city’s history and should be named within it.

Łódź’s remembrance developed through more than stone. Testimony, answers to inquiries, communal institutions and later memorial publications all carried memory forward. The Yiddish memorial book itself, published in Melbourne in 1974, belongs to that work: written from the perspective of survivors and former residents, it gathered accounts of Jewish life before the war, its destruction and the difficult aftermath. Its voice is indispensable, but it speaks from a particular community and cannot stand for every survivor or every fate.

The [Łódź Jewish community](/communities/lodz/records/mention_7cf21187ba458875fe942af7) rebuilt institutions in the same city whose Jewish life had been violently shattered. To document testimony, respond to inquiries and propose a memorial were different tasks, but each resisted disappearance in its own way. Together they made remembrance an ongoing communal responsibility—one that remains open to further research into the commission’s surviving papers, the people who sought help, and the memorial proposal’s eventual history.
